title: Revised Memoir of Newton (Stukeley, diplomatic transcription)
author: William Stukeley
query_context: Newton Project text record for Stukeley memoir; checked the provenance header and the apple/gravity passage.
supports: Stukeley records a 1726 conversation in which Newton connected an apple falling perpendicularly with the thought of gravitation.
The passage describes Newton's reported reasoning from the Earth drawing the apple and the apple drawing the Earth.
limitations: This is a later memoir recording a recollection, not a contemporaneous 1665 laboratory or diary record.
It does not establish that an apple struck Newton, nor that one event alone caused the complete theory.
bounded_excerpt: the notion of gravitation came into his mind

title: Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton (Stukeley, normalized text)
author: William Stukeley
query_context: Newton Project normalized text and authorial provenance note.
supports: Stukeley presents the memoir as a mixture of his own knowledge and accounts he heard, and asks that Conduitt compare it.
The source therefore preserves an early witness report while explicitly exposing provenance and uncertainty.
limitations: The source's own caveat prevents treating every detail as an independently verified fact.
It cannot serve as a direct causal oracle for the formal predicate C(apple_fall, gravitational_theory).

title: Memoir of Newton by John Conduitt (fair copy)
author: John Conduitt
query_context: Newton Project normalized fair-copy text; catalogue metadata checked separately.
supports: Conduitt's early memoir repeats a report that Newton first thought of his system of gravity after observing an apple fall during the plague period.
limitations: Conduitt's text is a later memoir, not Newton's contemporaneous note.
It supplies provenance for a reported anecdote, not an experimentally controlled causal demonstration or a claim that the apple hit Newton.
bounded_excerpt: observing an apple fall from a tree

title: Newton: His Life and Work at a Glance
author: Newton Project
query_context: Timeline used to separate the reported apple anecdote from the later development and publication of the theory.
supports: The timeline presents the apple story as a later-reported anecdote and places the full formulation and Principia years after the plague-period return.
It records intervening work and correspondence rather than a single-event completion of the theory.
limitations: This is an institutional timeline, not a new primary source.
It does not adjudicate the exact causal weight of the apple observation.
bounded_excerpt: or so Newton himself is said to have claimed decades later

title: William Stukeley: Science, Religion and Archaeology in Eighteenth-Century England (Newton Project introduction)
author: David Boyd Haycock
query_context: Scholarly catalogue introduction used for the date and transmission context of Stukeley's account.
supports: The introduction places Stukeley's collection of memories in 1727 and identifies the later memoir as an early written vehicle for the apple anecdote.
It treats the story's transmission and possible self-fashioning as issues requiring historical judgment.
limitations: This is secondary contextual material and cannot replace the underlying memoirs.
It does not turn the anecdote into a measured causal finding.
